The Fifth-Generation MINI Cooper 3-Door and John Cooper Works GP Are Live, Though Only Virtually
9 photos
Photo: uygarspots / Instagram
The iconic British marque Mini has two stories: the classic and modern ones. The legendary Mini, the one we all associate with the crowded streets of London and Mr. Bean, lived from 1959 to 2000, up to the Mark VII incarnation, along with many variants.
The modern story began with the acquisition of the MINI name by the premium Bavarian automaker BMW AG to form a potent triumvirate with the MINI brand as the opening act, the namesake BMW marque as the stable housemate, and Rolls-Royce sitting at the top.
Naturally, MINI developed itself around the classic hatchback, which was reinvented for the modern age – albeit with the same signature traits. The first generation came in 2001, the second iteration in 2006, and the third one in 2013, all of them deeply and intimately connected to each other through an evolutionary design ethos.
However, the current fourth generation presented in late 2023 broke off with tradition – it’s offered both in ICE and EV form, complete with visible design changes that make it a true modern-retro offering, and it’s easily recognizable via the simpler front fascia and the triangle-shaped LED rear lights compared to the previous incarnations.
The company offers three EV flavors – Cooper E, SE, and JCW Electric plus 1.5-liter or 2.0L turbo ICE options, along with three-door, five-door, and cabrio body styles. There’s Mini John Cooper Works for both types of powertrains, of course, and you would think that’s more than enough, at least for a few years, right?
Well, wrong – as the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators won’t stop dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI any time soon. For example, Uygar, a "professional daydreamer" based in Turkey and known as ' uygarspots ' on social media, has taken note of the all-new direction of MINI with the Cooper models and opted to imagine the next generation already!
He started fresh with a daring reinterpretation of the iconic model – the virtual artist keeps the overall shape along with the round headlights and the Union Jack motif of the taillights, but makes the MINI Cooper look ready for the 2030s. It’s all in the ‘pixels’, clearly, as now there are pixel-shaped round headlights, a pixel grille, as well as pixel-infused wheels and roofs!
The three-door model is also much wider now, giving space to a potential double-opening rear hatch – and you can also see the much larger Union Jack (British flag) LED taillights firmly occupy the space. The pixel master posts a few variants, as MINI always equals personalization, but more importantly, he comes back to also reveal his vision for the John Cooper Works GP, a true hot hatchback, even if it’s all electric. Matilda Is an Aussie-Built Sprinter That Makes Long Off-Grid Trips Feel Like a Luxury Stay
19 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia
North America is packed with companies that create awesome adventure-ready camper vans. If you were to go someplace else to find a similar level of quality, my best bet would be Australia - Aussies really know how to transform vehicles into adventure-ready homes on wheels, as proven by the variety of builds you can find on the market. Today, I'm checking out a fresh conversion that nicely balances ruggedness and comfort.
Meet Matilda, a build based on a 2025 AWD Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 144" wheelbase and a high roof. It was created by Summit Vans, an Australia-based company specializing in camper vans built on the Sprinter platform.
This rig is definitely an eye-catcher, not only because it's finished in a beautiful Pebble Grey paint, but also because it sports a variety of exterior mods .
For instance, you can tell this rig was designed with off-roading in mind due to its wheel and tire combo - it rides on black Summit Vans wheels wrapped in Toyo Open Country all-terrain tires.
Before it made any modification or addition to the van, Summit Vans did a GVM (Gross Vehicle Mass) upgrade that offers an extra 727 lb. (330 kg) of payload capacity for a total of 9,766 lb. (4,430 kg). It comprises an upgraded rear leaf spring and an Outback bracket reinforcement. The van also sports Falcon adjustable shocks.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia Cars and vans already have a high chance of suffering paint chips and scratches when driving normally. When going off the beaten path, they're basically unavoidable. That's why many builders opt to coat certain elements in truck bed liner.
On this van, the bumpers, the grille, and side rocker panels are coated in Raptor liner. A nice aesthetic touch is that the badges are satin black. Furthermore, at the rear, Summit Vans installed a step and a spare tire carrier/ladder combo.
A van's roof offers valuable space that can be used for storage or for attaching accessories. On top of this rig, you'll come across a Weldbeat rack that holds a Fiamma awning, a front-facing Lightforce LED light bar, and two 200 W solar panels. The roof is also prepped for the installation of a Starlink Mini antenna.
Like many premium Sprinter-based camper vans, this rig sports a set of flares. Flares, also known as pods or capsules, are designed to increase the van width to allow you to fit a bed in an east to west arrangement.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia Flares are so popular on Sprinters because the model is slightly narrower than other camper van base vehicle options, like the Ford Transit or the Ram ProMaster. This van's Summit flares are coated in Raptor liner and come with half-slider windows. Other notable exterior mods are power and water connections and Weldbeat side steps.
Inside is the even more impressive bit. Slide the door open and a tastefully designed, space-maximizing interior will greet you. It has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space.
The open layout is super useful despite you losing some privacy and insulation, as it lets you use the cabin not just when driving. What makes this possible is the fact that the driver and passenger seats are mounted on swivel bases.
Regarding aesthetics, the customer opted for wall panels upholstered in grey woven outdoor fabric, dark grey laminated cabinetry, a slatted bamboo ceiling with recessed LED light strips, and warm wood-imitating vinyl plank flooring.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia Dead ahead of the entrance, Summit Vans added one of the two kitchen units. It offers a decent amount of counter space and integrates a 130-liter Dometic fridge with a tiny freezer compartment.
Above the counter, you get a microwave oven and the "command center" for the rig's utilities. The latter includes a thermostat, a touchscreen display that lets you monitor and control the power and water systems, dimmer light switches, and switches for a water pump, shower fan, and more.
The other kitchen unit is on the passenger side, by the entrance. It features a deep black stainless steel sink and a sizeable countertop. You can use a portable stove for cooking, and a Maxxair vent fan will draw out the smells and fumes from cooking.
Five drawers and a cabinet underneath the sink are available for storage. Moreover, the largest kitchen drawer can double as a step to climb into bed.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia On the opposite side, you'll find a surprisingly roomy bathroom behind a tall mirror door. It boasts a shower with a handheld wand, a wall-integrated vent, and an OGO Origin composting toilet. It also has an all-white aesthetic with white acrylic walls.
The bathroom doubles as a drying room for your gear, as it has a duct that pumps hot air into the space. What's more, there are L-Tracks that let you easily hang your items for drying - you can also use them to attach a clothesline.
You get a comfy bedroom all the way back inside the van. It has a cozy setup with two overhead cabinets with bamboo sliding steps, L-Tracks on the walls, and a ceiling A/C unit that can quickly cool off the interior when needed.
The space underneath the bedroom serves as a garage that's accessible from both inside and outside the van. Two tall boxes on the sides offer additional storage space and accommodate the utility systems.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia Loading and unloading items was made as easy as possible thanks to a pull-out tray with heavy-duty slides. Moreover, two rear door gas struts make it easier for you to pop the doors open and prevent them from slamming shut or hitting the sides of the van.
Power is on the left side – the electrical system's highlights are two 410 Ah batteries and a 3,000 W inverter. Three charging sources help keep the batteries topped off at all times: solar power , shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a freshwater tank, an under-mounted greywater tank, a water filtration system, and an outdoor shower connection. A Dieselheat DH9 hydronic system provides both hot water and heated air.
All in all, Matilda by Summit Vans blends a calm, natural interior with a roam-ready exterior setup. Long trips will be a breeze in this camper van thanks to the myriad of creature comforts and systems.

RevoZport Ignores the new BMW X5, Launches Tuning Kit for the F95 X5 M
7 photos
Photo: Instagram | revozport
There’s an entirely new BMW X5 out, and in case you somehow missed it, then you should continue to ignore it.
After all, it’s a Neue Klasse model, which means that it looks horrible both inside and out, this writer believes, and just like me, I’m convinced that most petrolheads feel the same. The G65 debuted earlier this year. It hit the assembly line at Spartanburg, in South Carolina, a couple of months ago, and it is also assembled in China, albeit only for the LWB (long wheelbase) that it marketed locally.
The new-gen BMW X5 is based on an updated version of the CLAR platform, so despite the new skin and ultra high-tech interior that will age pretty much like a smartphone, it still shares its nuts and bolts with the G11 7 Series, G15 8 Series, G06 X6, G07 X7, and the XM. The old X5 is also based on the same construction, in case you forgot, and so is its range-topping version, the X5 M, and this story is dedicated to this exact model.
More particularly, it is all about the one pictured above in the gallery, which came directly from RevoZport’s portfolio. The tuner founded more than two decades ago and primarily located in Hong Kong, albeit with operations worldwide, including the United States of America, recently shared images of this modified vehicle on its social media channels, refraining from saying a lot of things about it, and stating it it wears its “street kit.”
Photo: Instagram | revozport The body kit targets the LCI, which is Bimmer slang for facelift and stands for Life Cycle Impulse, version of the F95 BMW X5 M , and makes it look a bit more aggressive. At the front, we can see that this ride features new trim on the side vents, as well as a sharped apron attached to the OEM bumper. The grille surrounds are thicker, so we reckon they have come from RevoZport’s portfolio, too, and so has the hood, with its vented and a lot more aggressive design.
From what we can tell, the wheel arch trim appears to be the same, so there are no fender flares here that would have made the entire thing a bit wider compared to the stock one. The side skirts, on the other hand, have come from the aftermarket world, just like the rear diffuser. The roof-mounted wing looks the same as the OEM element to us, and so does the rear bumper. The door mirror casings also carry over, and the exhaust tips look just as big as the stock ones.
You do know that no tuning job would be complete these days without an aftermarket set of wheels, don’t you? And while we’d like to tell you that the pictured BMW X5 M also ticks this box, we can’t, because the alloys are not fully visible. Thus, we could be looking at the OEM ones, as these are just as big as far as we can tell, though we could be wrong, as they might be new. But do they look like they are part of the tuning job to you?
Photo: Instagram | revozport Before revealing your answer and speaking your mind about this build in the comments box below, we have to tell you that this machine features a satin black look on the outside, and retains its Bimmer roundels at the front and rear, as well as the M logos. The cockpit is not visible at all, though such a thing would look best with black leather upholstery and a few touches of suede here and there, as well as the usual amount of carbon fiber trim.
We cannot tell you whether the engine has been upgraded, but our bet would be on the word “no.” This would mean that the 4.40-liter S68 powering the facelifted iteration of the BMW X5 M , and featuring mild-hybrid assistance, would still develop 617 hp (625 ps/460 kW) at a screaming 6,000 rpm, and 553 pound-feet (750 Nm) of torque between 1,800 and 5,860 rpm. With no outside intervention, this model needs just 3.9 seconds to hit 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill, and that makes it just a few tenths of a second slower than the iconic Ferrari Enzo.
The performance is definitely something to write home about, because we are talking about a premium mid-size crossover with plenty of space inside. And for what it’s worth, the F95 BMW X5 M, just like the regular G05 X5, have aged like fine wine rather than fine milk, and they are some of the best-looking machines in their class, this writer believes. I want to say the same about the modern-day X5 (and X5 M) a few years from now, but I doubt that it would start growing on me, especially with that soulless interior.
Now, do you dig the makeover of this BMW X5 M , or would you have yours bone stock? I lean on the latter rather than the former, but the tuning job is definitely not bad at all. View this post on Instagram A post shared by RevoZport (@revozportt)

Car Nut Put 1985 Chevy K20 on 44-Inch Rubbers To Leave Kids in Awe at Shows, Never Drives It on Dirt
49 photos
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower
Typically, when we look at a pickup truck with big tires, hockey puck-sized tread blocks, high road clearance, and a beefy rear diff, we instinctively think “Off-Road.” After all, what’s the purpose of a lifted utilitarian, if not to go over ravines and ditches and rocks and stuff that’s doesn’t reside on the blacktop? I’ll tell you what: the fun of it. Josh Anderson, from Franklin, Tennessee, put his square-body K20 on 44-inch rubbers just because he likes the look of it.
Raising pickup trucks purely for recreation began in rural America during the 1970s, evolving from utilitarian necessity into a flamboyant subculture of mechanical one-upmanship. Southern and Midwestern drivers originally elevated four-wheel-drive workhorses to clear deep ruts, swamplands, bogs, agricultural mud holes, fallen trees, deep fords, and whatever Mother Nature had planted in their paths.
Soon, young enthusiasts realized that towering suspension lifts delivered unmatched street presence, turning functional farm rigs into flashy Saturday night cruisers built solely for visual drama and youthful rebellion.
That skyward obsession fueled the parallel culture of big-inch tires on pickups. In 1973, builders scoured commercial catalogs for 12-by-16.5-inch highway rubber before Dick Cepek popularized wide off-road floatation tires and Bob Chandler created Bigfoot on 66-inch terra tires. After Interco launched its aggressive Super Swamper tread in 1978, pairing 15-inch steel wheels with bulbous 44-inch bias-ply mud tires defined classic four-wheel-drive proportions.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower That was long before flashy modern 22-inch rims appeared, which are absolutely frowned upon by old-schoolers who think there’s nothing better than lifting your truck with the sole purpose of making an entrance in big style (pun intended), and leaving life-long memories to rugrats who come to a car show and are left with their tiny jaws dangling three thirty-seconds of a inch above the ground when sitting next to the giant pickup towering above all else.
Preserving that golden era of sidewall-heavy Americana is what Erik Larsen, the man behind the camera on the Heart and Horsepower YouTube channel, brought in front of the entire internet in his latest episode. The feature spotlights Josh Anderson of Franklin, Tennessee, and his majestic 1985 Chevrolet K20 Scottsdale pickup, built solely to honor his 1990s high school youth.
"I wanted the truck to be exactly the way it would have been when I remember these trucks rolling around," Anderson explains with a nostalgic flashback to an age when having fun meant busting knuckles and going on a full analog search of parts, with a lot of physical travel involved.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower Long before it towered above traffic, this pickup started out in life as a stock 1985 Chevrolet K20 Scottsdale three-quarter-ton, four-wheel-drive Fleetside work truck. Remarkably, its original buyer commissioned the pickup in Colorado Gold Metallic, a rare special-order factory finish designated by paint code 51 and WA7953 that dealers almost never stocked.
Anderson tracked the survivor down in Gruetli-Laager, Tennessee, a remote mountain community atop Monteagle Mountain (some two hours away from Franklin, and about 40 miles north west of Chattanooga), and bought it. The rest he did himself.
The Chevrolet C/K moniker debuted for the 1960 model year, using “C” for two-wheel-drive models and “K” for four-wheel-drive trucks, paired with 10, 20, and 30 capacity ratings. Production spanned four generations from 1960 through 2002: the first from 1960 to 1966, the second from 1967 to 1972, the third from 1973 to 1991, and the fourth from 1988 to 2002, totaling over twenty million C/K trucks built across its lifespan.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower General Motors officially dubbed the third-generation trucks the Rounded Line, though enthusiasts universally call the 1973 to 1987 pickups “Square Bodies,” with R/V badging continuing on specialty models through 1991. Total third-generation output exceeded 10,000,000 units, opening with 666,619 Chevrolet trucks in 1973 and peaking in 1978 when division volume hit 1,317,466.
For 1985, Chevrolet built over 650,000 C/K pickups, including roughly 48,000 K20 trucks and 30,000 military K-series utility pickups. Because General Motors never archived complete 1985 K20 production totals broken down by individual option codes, historians analyze the model year through factory configuration matrices.
Buyers in 1985 selected from three trim levels: utilitarian Custom Deluxe, mid-tier Scottsdale, and top-spec Silverado, with Scottsdale and Silverado representing roughly 75 percent of sales. All K20 pickups of 1985 used a 131.5-inch wheelbase as two-door regular cabs with 8-foot Fleetside, Stepside, or chassis-cab bodies.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower Straight-sided Fleetside beds represented over 85 percent of 1985 K20 output, while 164.5-inch-wheelbase four-door Bonus and Crew Cab bodies were reserved for C20, C30, and K30 chassis. Factory 1985 C/K engines included two Sixes (the 155-hp 4.3-liter V6, and a 115-horsepower 4.8-liter inline-6), and four V8s.
The entry-level motor was a 160-horsepower 5.0-liter V8 (307 cubic inches), followed by volume-leading 165-horsepower 5.7-liter V8 (Chevy’s long-standing 350 small-block), accompanied by a 130-horsepower 6.2-liter diesel V8. The lineup was completed by the 230-horse 7.4-liter V8 (the famous 454 big-block). Transmission-wise, the C/Ks of ’85 came paired with 4-speed manuals, or 3- and 4-speed automatics.
Working solo inside his garage, Anderson completed the entire frame-up transformation, bodywork, and fresh Colorado Gold paint in just 4 months. To achieve its period-correct altitude, he installed 12-inch Superlift leaf springs alongside a 3-inch body lift, revised shock mounts, dual steering stabilizers, and transfer case drops. Beneath the fenders sit 44-inch Super Swamper Bogger bias-ply tires mounted on 15-by-15-inch black steelies.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower
"I've always thought you had to have a bigger tire than you did wheel," Anderson says of his 15-inch rims, noting that when 22-inch wheels arrived, "that's the day that I knew that four-wheel drives were going south." Inflated to 12 psi, the bias-ply Boggers flat-spot when parked for months. "You better pay attention. It steers like it looks. It takes a 40-acre field to turn it around," he laughs. But hey, you can fist-bump semi drivers and look them dead in the eye without raising your chin.
To turn that massive unsprung weight, Anderson replaced the original engine with a 385-cubic-inch small-block Chevrolet stroker V8 topped by an Edelbrock intake, paired with a 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic 350 automatic transmission and a gear-driven New Process 205 transfer case. "To pull these big tires around, you got to have something a little bit different. This truck runs and drives good at 60 mph all day long," he proudly notes.
Photo: YouTube/Heart and Horsepower It can’t imagine what it’s like going 60 on tarmac with those rubbers clunking along. The builder/owner never even thinks about going off asphalt. That’s not what his truck was built for. It’s a statement of skill and personal preference, not a tool to haul logs or bags of hog feed up and down the mountain. Impressing kids at car meets – yes. Actually using it to its full capacity – never. He just put it on grass for the sake of cinematic good looks, but that's about as far as he will go with it.
Instead, it recreates the Saturday nights he spent cruising with his wife in high school and delights children at car shows, whom he gladly invites up in the cab (he probably has a ladder with him for that). And yet, after all the work put into it, Josh Anderson doesn’t hesitate a fraction of a second when asked about selling it : "The only reason I'd sell it is because I know if I wanted another, I'd just build another." Which would also keep his passion alive.

Someone Paid Less Than Two iPhones for This BMW 335i xDrive Sedan
14 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
The E9X-generation BMW 3 Series goes for virtually nothing these days, as it’s worth pennies on the dollar compared to what it used to cost back when it was in production, and if you ever dreamed about getting one of these, then this is a good time to finally take that step.
Take the car pictured above, for example, which recently sold for nothing, and it’s not really a base model either. In fact, you are looking at the 335i xDrive flavor, meaning that it left the assembly line rocking a twin-turbocharged straight-six 3.0-liter engine. The N54 produced 300 hp (304 ps/224 kW) at 5,800 rpm and 300 pound-feet (407 Nm) of torque when the car was new. The mill is paired with a six-speed manual transmission, and rear-biased xDrive all-wheel drive.
From 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph), the 2009 model year BMW 335i xDrive Sedan needed 5.5 seconds, and its top speed was electronically limited to 155 mph (250 kph). Besides the stick shift, this model was also available with a six-speed automatic transmission. And in case you forgot, the 335i bridged the gap between the regular 3 Series and the M3. And the latter came with a 4.0-liter V8 engine back then, making 414 hp (420 ps/309 kW) and 295 lb-ft (400 Nm) of torque. This was the only M3 offered with a V8.
Due to some of the mods, this BMW M335i xDrive Sedan should have more oomph, though since a dyno chart does not accompany the ad, we do not know the revised numbers. Speaking of the modifications, these include the new intakes, downpipes, exhaust system, charge pipes, blow-off valve, an intercooler, and an oil cooler, as well as ignition coils, and a custom tune.
Photo: Cars&Bids These are joined by the Bilstein struts, a set of lowering springs, and 17-inch wheels painted black. The black kidney grilles, door mirrors, ducktail spoiler, darkened headlights and taillights, new badges, shift knob, and steering wheel also came from the aftermarket world, the listing reveals.
The heated seats, power sunroof, Dakota leather upholstery, walnut wood trim, and automatic climate control are the OEM features mentioned in the ad.
We will need a much longer paragraph to discuss the known flaws, because this old BMW 3 Series was involved in an accident in August 2017, sustaining damage to the back end. Chips and scratches on the outside, a crank on the front bumper vent, curb rash and scuffs on the wheels, creases and wear on the seats, wear on interior touch points, and a damaged left rear door panel are also mentioned in the ad.
Moreover, the premium compact sports sedan in question also has washer fluid and tire pressure monitoring warning lights on, a missing engine valve cover, a misaligned front intercooler blamed on a damaged plastic engine splash shield, and the right rear door does not open. Thus, the new owner has plenty of things to fix if they want their Bimmer to shine.
Photo: Cars&Bids The valve cover was replaced in June 2025, at 100,062 miles (161,034 km), the engine oil and filter were changed in August 2022, at 76,242 miles (122,700 km), in April 2022, and in August 2021, and an alignment was performed in August 2022. The seller said that the spark plugs, spark plug wires, intercooler, intercooler piping, alternator belt, pulley, and fuel sender unit, as well as the CV axles, battery, and four tires were replaced in 2025 and 2026, though no documentation has been provided.
As you already know, this BMW 3 Series is not exactly a low mileage example. The odometer read 105,300 miles (169,500 km) at the time of cataloging, and this Bimmer, with its black-on-black look, has a clean Florida title. This Is Oblio, a Warm and Functional Bus Home DIYed by the "Grandmaster Skoolie Builder" Himself
22 photos
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot
If you're a bus lifer, a DIYer in the process of building your own school bus home, or simply a fan of skoolie conversions, you’ve probably heard of Chuck Cassady. The man is a legend in the world of bus living. Known to many as the Grandmaster Skoolie Builder, he has spent nearly a decade honing his skills, helping others build their mobile homes, and sharing what he has learned through online videos.
Cassady ran a bus conversion company for almost a decade, appeared on several TV shows, and published around 200 YouTube videos to help people complete their own DIY skoolie projects. Today, I’m going to take a closer look at the second bus home he built for himself from scratch, a gorgeous build he christened Oblio.
Based on a decommissioned school bus he bought in May 2021, Oblio showcases Chuck’s craftsmanship, technical knowledge, and attention to detail, combining practical design with a livable layout, beautiful finishes, and reliable systems for off-grid living.
As Chuck himself confesses in the video attached below, his journey into skoolie life began out of necessity in 2015. He was in college back then and he couldn’t afford rent, so he decided to live in his first bus, which he lovingly called Queen of Peace. He knew little about building at the time, but he was willing to learn and the experience helped him gain new skills. Things eventually evolved into a skoolie building business, and then he also started a YouTube channel to share all the knowledge he has gained along the way.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot Oblio is the second bus he builds for himself. It’s based on a 1996 International chassis fitted with a Thomas school bus body and measures 27.5 feet (8.4 meters) long. It’s way shorter than Chuck’s previous 38-foot (11.5-meter) bus conversion, but what draw him in was the engine. The school district had installed a new Cummins engine in 2018, shortly before the bus left service, and it’s the kind of engine you typically find in larger 40-foot (12.2-meter) school buses. And the best part, it only had about 30,000 miles (48,280 km) on it when he purchased it.
He still made a few modifications to the mechanical part, like installing a larger radiator, changing the transmission, and replacing every hose and belt, before beginning the actual conversion process.
To make it more comfortable to live in full time, Chuck raised the roof by 12 inches (30 cm), which resulted in more headroom inside, and replaced the original school bus windows with RV windows. He also painted the bus’s exterior is a pleasant olive green shade that allows it to blend in with natural environments.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot He also built three storage bays that carry his tools, outdoor equipment, and personal belongings, and added as many solar panels as he could fit on the roof to support off-grid living. At the rear of the bus, the doors open to reveal a huge garage area that holds a 125-gallon (473-liter) freshwater tank, the water heater, and the power system components.
But Chuck’s excellent craftsmanship and efficient use of space are more noticeable inside Oblio, where he created an open living space with a front lounge, a dinette, a central kitchen, a separate bathroom, and a rear bedroom. Since the school bus is shorter, he had to fit everything inside a compact floor plan, but he definitely made every inch count. On top of that, the use of warm wood finishes, curved cabinetry, and discreet lighting gives it a warm, cozy feel.
The choice of materials played an important role in how welcoming the interior feels. Cedar closet liner was used on the curved ceiling, the countertops are made from Richlite, a durable material made from compressed paper, and Marmoleum covers the floor. Marmoleum is also a durable, waterproof material made from 97% natural materials, including crushed limestone, linseed oil, wood flour, and jute. Oak details add even more warmth, and the rounded edges also soften the interior.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot At the front of the bus, Chuck installed a new driver’s seat but still has to redo the dash area. But as you step into the actual habitat, the first area is the lounge, which is also his office, dining space, and everyday living area. He furnished it with a custom sofa and a separate dinette for two.
To help maintain an organized, uncluttered interior, he had to come up with clever storage solutions, so upper shelves run along both sides of the interior, the dinette is raised to create storage underneath, the seating benches have built-in drawers, and the table also has a small slide-out junk drawer underneath. Even the sofa has hidden storage behind its cushions.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot Moving further into the bus, we discover the kitchen, which features a long Richlite countertop, walnut cabinet fronts, and a tiled backsplash finished with epoxy grout. He equipped the cooking area with an induction cooktop, an oven, and a large undercounter marine-style refrigerator. A pull-out pantry and numerous drawers provide plenty of space for pots, pottery, utensils, and supplies. A separate cabinet integrates a stainless-steel undermount sink with a foot-pedal faucet.
Despite the bus’s modest dimensions, Chuck wanted a proper bathroom, so he built an elongated space with a large shower, a custom vanity with curved edges, an asymmetrical backlit mirror, and a composting toilet. The whole bathroom has tile walls, while the exterior curved wall is decorated with a flowery wallpaper.
The rear of the skoolie is Chuck’s bedroom. It features a raised fixed bed flanked by two opening windows and with a curved illuminted shelf surrounding it. A pair of storage stairs makes climbing into bed easier, and beside the bed, there is a wardrobe with a nifty tray-like nightstand area above it, perfect for keeping books, remote controls, gadgets, and other knick-knacks.
Photo: Mobile Dwellings/YouTube screenshot According to Chuck, Oblio was built to support an off-grid lifestyle, though the power system capacity is not mentioned. The main idea, however, is that this skoolie gives him the freedom to travel and help other people with their own projects.
In terms of costs, the bus itself was $5,500, and though Chuck didn’t keep a record of everything he purchased for the build, he estimates he spent about $60,000 on materials. He also put between 800 to 1,000 work hours into the build.

source_document.body:
The NHTSA has proposed using cyan-colored lights to identify vehicles operating autonomously, along with other additions to get ready for autonomous vehicles.
As the autonomous vehicles start to spread on US roads, questions have come up about how to deal with these new driverless vehicles.
One question involves emergency response – not only do the vehicles need to be prepared to respond to emergency personnel, those personnel need to recognize when a car is operating autonomously. A police officer needs to know that nobody’s in the driver seat, or an emergency responder needs to know that if there’s nobody in the driver’s seat, that’s not necessarily because there’s a missing driver somewhere who needs rescue.
These are just some of the reasons one might want to know whether a car is operating autonomously, but as of yet, there is no standardized messaging to suggest that a vehicle is doing so.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
This week, NHTSA proposed an answer. In a draft proposal released Friday , it suggested a whole new color for vehicle lamps, cyan, to signal autonomous operation.
The proposal was actually first put forward by Mercedes, alongside its DRIVE PILOT level 3 driver assist system. This is the first true hands-free system offered in the US, which allows drivers to forgo responsibility for the car under certain conditions, and let the car truly drive itself. This differs from systems like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, which is actually only a “level 2” system, where the driver is still responsible when the system is on.
We tried Mercedes’ system out in Santa Monica traffic , and were impressed at how quickly we adjusted to our temporary robotic chauffer.
When we saw that system, we also saw Mercedes’ proposal for lighting: cyan lights around the exterior of the vehicle, denoting autonomous operation.
Unfortunately our demo was on a bright sunny day (a necessity to operate the level 3 system, which doesn’t run at night or in bad weather), so the lights didn’t pop as much as they might have in lower light, but you get the drift.
Mercedes trialed the system in California for two years, and it seems the NHTSA is happy with the results, since it is proposing to take the idea national (after input from the SAE, which also likes the idea of using cyan).
The new draft regulation would allow for optional inclusion of cyan lights, but would not require them. So, it’s entirely possible that automakers would decide to save the small cost that it would take to engineer and include these lights.
But by putting the idea out into the regulations, it gets everyone thinking about a future where this color might be required (and I could see that requirement coming quite quickly) – so automakers are likely to start thinking of where these lights would go, and including them, since LEDs don’t really cost anything anyway.
The regulation states that the lights should turn on when the car is operating autonomously, and turn off when it isn’t – they should never be on when a driver is actively driving the vehicle. They should all turn on and off simultaneously, and they should be visible from any angle, with markers on the front, sides and rear, all at least 15 inches off the ground.
China just announced essentially the same regulation earlier this week. The country released a draft standard that would take effect in 2028, is optional, and uses turquoise as its proposed color. This, too, was a reaction to the proliferation of lights on autonomous vehicles in China, and the government has asked automakers to stop doing their own thing and instead follow the new standardized system.
The NHTSA’s draft regulation covers several other aspects of autonomous vehicle operation, mostly by updating Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) rules to allow some flexibility for certain operations that won’t be used by autonomous vehicles.
For example, cars are required to have a turn signal that turns off automatically after the steering wheel turns beyond a certain threshold and then returns back to neutral. That wouldn’t apply to cars without steering wheels, so the updated rules delete that requirement for autonomous cars. It also changes certain headlight requirements for more design flexibility.
Electrek’s Take
While I’ve got a lot to say about the corrupt reality TV character running the DoT, and how he’s trying to raise your energy costs and kill children on bicycles , this autonomous vehicle regulation is a long time coming and is needed.
There are still some careerists in the NHTSA who take their job seriously, and are pushing regulations like this, and we can be thankful that not all of them have been forced out by the rampant corruption the US is seeing right now.
That said, the loosening of rules for autonomous vehicles is something we need to keep our eye on. Certain things, like allowing reasonable changes to FMVSS rules for things that really make no sense for an AV (like the turn signal change, or various required driver displays), are totally reasonable.
But it’s also hard not to look at this and say, well, could the guy who has given hundreds of millions in bribes to try to cancel investigations against him and wants to sell you an unusable car without a steering wheel be behind any of this?
After all, that steering-wheel-less car was subject to an immediate NHTSA investigation when it was suddenly put into service without forewarning, with the NHTSA pointing out myriad problems . Changing the rules after the fact to accompany a vehicle that already violated them doesn’t set great precedent.
So… we can be happy for the adaptation to new technology, but still need to ensure that safety is the North Star, rather than Mr. Musk’s fantasies. We have no specific reason in mind to oppose this specific regulation, but an environment so rife with corruption does not foster trust with the general populace, so here we are.

Restored 1963 Dodge W300 Power Wagon Sells for Record Price
14 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
Scheduled between October 21 and 24, Mecum's Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 auction brought hundreds of classics under the hammer. Among them, a 1963 Dodge Power Wagon that fetched over $100,000, the first of its kind to do so.
Introduced in 1945, the early Power Wagon was essentially a civilian version of the military WC series. However, the lineup expanded to include various haulers over the years. In 1957, Dodge debuted both light- and medium-duty trucks with the Power Wagon moniker.
The green pickup you see here is a W300 version, which makes it a one-ton vehicle. The truck shares styling cues with the first-generation D Series (1961-1965), but it has a taller body. In this case, it also rides higher and features all-wheel drive.
The truck crossed the auction block for $110,000, making it by far the most expensive of its kind ever sold at public auction. I do need to add that I'm only talking about factory-stock examples; restomods tend to fetch a lot more. The previous record was set by a 1963 WM300 that fetched $53,000.
What made enthusiasts bid this truck into six-figure territory? Well, for starters, they're pretty rare. While Dodge sold quite a few of them back in the day, these Power Wagons were treated like workhorses and discarded into junkyards once they weren't worth repairing. Trucks in such outstanding condition are hard to come by.
This example received a frame-off, nut-and-bolt restoration that was completed in 2019. It was repainted in the original code-51 Pine Green color, while the cabin had nearly everything either restored or replaced. Some of the body panels are also replaced with parts from other trucks due to severe rust.
The engine bay, which was also refinished, hides a 318-cubic-inch (5.2-liter) small-block V8 engine. There's no info on whether it's numbers-matching, but it's definitely period-correct. The mill delivered 215 horsepower in these trucks at the time (and 230 horsepower in passenger cars). The 318 V8 was optional, as the Power Wagon came standard with a slant-six .
The mill mates with a four-speed NP420 synchro-shift manual transmission, a two-speed transfer case, and a limited-slip differential with 4.88 gears. The truck is fitted with the Utiline Stepside nine-foot bed. The Power Wagon was reportedly kept in a garage since the restoration, and the odometer shows 70,513 miles (113,480 km).
As of this writing, this truck is among the top 10 most expensive (factory-stock) classic cars sold at Dallas/Fort Worth 2026. The list is topped by a 1968 Shelby GT500 ($154,000), a 1969 Dodge Super Bee A12 ($151,250), and a 1969 Shelby GT500 ($140,250). As far as restomods go, a 1963 Chevrolet Corvette changed hands for $297,000, while a 1963 Bel Air fetched $214,500. What's your take on this gorgeous pickup truck?

Time Capsule 1940 Buick Super Phaeton Is Hen's Teeth Rare, Owner's Afraid To Drive It, Wants To Sell
63 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Going for a top-down ride with the family is an utopia in today’s environment (sadly crowded with SUVs and pickup trucks, or oversized sedans and wagons – though these last two are getting rarer by the day). Two seats – or at the best two and two halves in the back – it not really family-friendly, is it? I’m talking taking the lady and the kids (three or more) out for ice cream on a lovely Saturday noon. But back in 1940, this was a very handy possibility. Say “Hi” to one of the rarest cars on Planet Piston, a 1940 Buick Super Phaeton 51C.
Phaeton designated four doors and a convertible top – something unconceivable by today’s standards (unless it’s a Jeep Wrangler or a Ford Bronco). Well, Buick – and pretty much everyone else before the war – had other ideas. Good ideas. Great, even. Fantastic, in fact. The last American car to sport this particular body style was the glorious Lincoln Continental of 1961-1967. I mean proper car, not SUV or anything of that sort.
But dial back the wheels of time to 1940, and the roads show a different picture entirely – one where six people could ride in comfort and in style in a magnificent drophead like a Buick Super Series 50. Few American nameplates capture 1940s upper-middle-class aspiration quite like Buick’s Super. Although the Flint automaker first used the Series 50 designation between 1930 and 1935 (on 127,416 cars, mind you) the “Super” moniker debuted for the 1940 model year.
Spanning five distinct generations, the classic lineage endured until 1958, pausing only from 1943 to 1945, before briefly returning from 2008 to 2009 on V8-powered luxury performance sedans.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Conceived as an ingenious bridge within the General Motors hierarchy, the original Super paired the cavernous new C-body torpedo shell of the senior Roadmaster with the economical powertrain of the entry-level Special. Buyers embraced this formula during the first generation from 1940 to 1941, driving total generational output to 220,803 automobiles, split between an impressive 128,736 units produced for the 1940 model year and 92,067 additional examples built during 1941.
Riding on a 121-inch wheelbase, the 1940 Series 50 lineup offered five body styles: a four-door touring sedan, a two-door sport coupe, a two-door convertible coupe, a four-door estate wagon, and the flagship Model 51C four-door convertible phaeton. In earnest, the brochure advertised just the first two when the model year lineup was presented to the public. The two- and four-door convertibles and the wagon were introduced later in the season.
Priced at $1,549 for the phaeton, the Super battled a heavy array of domestic rivals including the Packard One-Twenty and One-Eighty, Oldsmobile Series 90, Hudson Custom Eight and Deluxe Six, and Mercury Eight. Cadillac and LaSalle (Series Sixty-Two and Series 50, respectively), also had a go at the body style, but didn’t keep it for long.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Every 1940 Super carried a 248-cubic-inch (4.1-liter) Dynaflash overhead-valve straight-eight engine featuring a 6.1:1 compression ratio, and a two-barrel carburetor to deliver 107 horsepower at 3,400 rpm and 203 lb-ft of torque at 2,000 rpm, paired only with a 3-speed manual transmission. It was more than enough muscle to move 3,900 lb of Buick Phaeton (1.8 tons), and it is plenty power to put one down the road even 86 years after it rolled off the assembly line.
A museum-grade time capsule from that inaugural 1940 campaign took center stage on Lou Costabile’s YouTube episode of “My Car Story” series. The avid Chicago-based vlogger and all-around classic car documentarist got the ride of a lifetime in Dennis Doerge’s “1940 Buick Super Model 51C four-door convertible phaeton” in July. The video just dropped, though, se we can all enjoy the memories of summer breezes just as Halloween is about to trick-or-treat.
Well, it’s a treat for us for sure, and a double home run for the youtuber: not only did he ride in one of the last surviving examples of the 1940 Buick Super 51-C Sport Phaeton, he also got to enjoy the ride in Dennis Doerge’s example, which is a blue moon situation in itself. Although the Buick collector has many other classics that he drives without hesitation, this one only comes out when the weather is perfect, and only to car shows. When this classic gets driven, hens make dentist appointments.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile It's one of just 1,351 examples built, and one of less than ten believed by marque specialists to survive today. If 1,351 sounds like a lot, consider that it was the grand total of Phaetons built by Buick on all its series (40,50, 60, 70, 80, and 90). The 51-C (the Super), saw a 534-strong production run in 1940, second only to the Series 40 (the Special), which saw 597 four-door ragtops assembled.
Doerge acquired the open-top Buick so many years ago that he no longer recalls the exact purchase date (it was around 2000), noting that its scarcity sealed the deal and that he has never encountered another example. Which is saying a lot (a lot of lots), considering Dennis’ extensive collection of rare cars (mostly Buicks), and his vast knowledge in the field.
Treated to a concourse frame-off restoration leaving its undercarriage as spotless as its exterior, the car earned a 2010 National First Prize and Senior Grand National award, accumulating just 85 miles on its odometer since restoration completion.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Finished in deep maroon with pinstriped wheels, wide whitewalls, a 1940 California front plate, immaculate black rear stone guards, and cloisonné “Eight” emblems, the phaeton projects prewar grandeur like few cars do. The owner rarely lowers the tan canvas top because the heavy manual mechanism demands strenuous effort from two people. The power-assisted option was available back in 1940, but Dennis wasn’t picky when he found this one.
Raised, the roof imparts a limousine profile above a rounded trunk whose two-tier shelf houses a full-size spare wheel beneath surprisingly modest luggage space.
Inside, tan leather benches with a folding rear center armrest and chrome robe rail face an engine-turned dashboard housing a 110-mph speedometer and a Sonomatic push-button radio. Remarkably, a specialist fabricated every butterscotch knob and switch from scratch, from the throttle and ashtray pulls to the dash-top wiper control.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Although Doerge claimed everything worked except the passenger clock, Lou delightedly proved the timepiece was ticking and functioning properly. Speaking of which: in 1940, Buick claimed this about its eight-in-a-row.
“Pound for pound, this new 1940 Buick Dynaflash valve-in-head straight-eight engine is smoother than a high-grade watch." Such is the assurance given to President Curtice and Chief Engineer Chayne by the test they are observing here. Like every Buick engine for 1940, this one is electrically balanced to within a fraction of an inch-ounce.”
Closer inspection reveals thoughtful 1940 engineering touches throughout the cabin and bodywork. Ahead of the split V-windshield, whose rake Costabile likened to a streamlined diesel locomotive, sits a screened cowl ventilator paired with fender-mounted directional lamps. Inside, occupants benefit from dashboard windshield defroster slots, an under-dash fresh-air lever, and clustered gauges monitoring battery charge, coolant temperature, fuel level, oil pressure, and high-beam illumination via a bottom-mounted bright lights indicator window.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Pulling the chromed “Super” side badges unlatches a dual-hinged hood that opens from either flank, revealing an intriguing engineering quirk. While a solid metal shroud blocks the passenger side, a driver-side cutout grants access to the radiator cap and its reproduction methanol antifreeze tag. Between an AC oil filter and heavy-duty air cleaner, the engine block proudly displays the “1-6-2-5-8-3-7-4” firing order and “0.015-inch” hot valve clearance factory castings.
Once fired up, the 85-year-old inline-eight settles into a whisper-quiet idle through its chrome-tipped exhaust. Doerge candidly admits he is normally afraid to drive the trophy-winning phaeton, reserving it strictly for fair-weather show appearances.
Venturing onto sun-drenched Illinois country roads, the owner noted that the tires initially felt square from sitting stationary all winter, though the bias-ply rubber quickly rounded out to deliver a remarkably composed and velvet-smooth country ride.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Guided by its ivory banjo steering wheel and the crisp column-mounted 3-speed shifter, the torquey Buick accelerates briskly and cruises effortlessly at speeds of 60 to 70 mph. Both men marveled that a vehicle looking like a 6,000-pound behemoth actually weighs 3,900 pounds, relying on coil-sprung suspension and a traditional single-master-cylinder hydraulic drum braking system to slow down.
That tranquil country excursion also served as a bittersweet farewell lap for the 83-year-young owner. Having already sold eight collector vehicles over the winter while planning to part with 10 more as he trims his herd, Doerge revealed that this prized 1940 Buick Super Model 51C phaeton will soon seek a new custodian.
A discerning car nut will have the rare privilege of preserving a defining milestone of prewar American automotive history. If you're intereseted, drop a comment on Lou's YouTube channel (you might as well subscribe, too), and he'll put you in contact with the owner.

Porsche Mission RS Comes From Imagination Land, Ready to Make the New Supercar a Feisty Reality
8 photos
Photo: monacoautodesign / Instagram
Porsche is going through a bit of a bad streak in recent months, with dwindling sales in China, lower profits overall, plus a failure to make a dent in the EV field with the new Macan Electric. Now, on top of that, they also failed to see the lack of opportunity in overlapping a new model presentation with a Tesla launch.
China is not the paradise it used to be for premium Western automakers; abandoning the ICE Macan in favor of the EV one was a disaster, and Porsche also dropped the ICE 718 series from its roster – it’s only natural that its profits, along with sales, plunged globally. No worries, they have a new masterplan for the period until 2035.
It’s called ' Sportwagenschmiede 2035 ' and vacates 9k jobs to bring some economies to the finance department, but also comes with promises of the all-new 718 series with an electric platform that mimics a mid-engine setup, an upcoming Macan replacement – the so-called Project Octan, as well as hints of a possible large SUV coming above the current Cayenne and Cayenne Electric.
Most importantly, the new business plan teased an upcoming mid-engine ICE -powered sports car that will sit above the 911 series. Unfortunately for Porsche, they timed the presentation of the Mission S prototype quite wrong: it completely overlapped with the presentation of the latest Tesla, the wacky rocket-propelled Roadster .
No worries, as not everyone overlooked the Porsche Mission S in their quest to find out why the 2026 Tesla Roadster (which is actually coming out in 2028 at the earliest) is absolutely different compared to the Tesla Roadster presented in 2017, how did they fake (or not) those jumping party tricks, and how come a sports car is named a Roadster when there’s no drop-top.
Anyway, back to the Porsche, the Mission S was presented as the next step in volution for the brand in terms of mid-engine sports cars – though the company did refrain from saying what powers the new preview concept. Cue the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI.
They don’t really care about the powertrain, so here’s Brian Monaco, the automotive renderer and design advisor from West Palm Beach, FL (aka Monaco Auto Design ), who has some CGI thoughts about the new Porsche Mission S in terms of aerodynamics. In his vision, the new model should be called Porsche Mission RS and come with a glamorous neon yellow hue plus additional aerodynamic goodies.
Those include a complete kit done in exposed carbon fiber, packing a front spoiler, small dual canards on the bumper, and winglets both for the front and rear elements, plus a massive rear wing along with a carbon hood, roof, and the engine cover. There are also carbon fiber wheels with aerodisc covers around the back, and ‘RS’ labels on the rear part of the front fenders.
